Name: Ken Prince
Question: How do I travel for free?
Answer: I’ve seen plenty of people traveling around the world for free, they generally fall into a few archetypes. The Couch Surfer — This is the dude with a back pack and a pony tail who uses a website like Couch Surfing to travel all around the world without the expense of room and board. He can be found eating kale, doing yoga, and smoking marijuana when he’s not meditating. He’s almost a modern day hippy except much more confused. The Perfect Ten — This woman doesn’t just travel for free, she does everything for free. Her natural (and unnatural) beauty make her the belle of the ball—worldwide. She’s so gorgeous men pay for her flights, meals, shopping sprees, et al and ask nothing in return. The Trust Fund Baby—When I’m reincarnated I want to be reborn as a trust fund baby. You can find these guys and gals flying first class and you can spot them from a mile away—Rimowa luggage, dressed to impress, and slightly out of shape. Trust fund babies benefit from grandaddies hard work, and they live the good life—penthouses from OneFineStay and beach front mansions they found on AirBNB. The NGO / Activist / Non-Profit Causer— This person travels for free on the backs of selfless donors. They’re causers—so their entire self-worth is tied up in “saving the world” and other nefarious activities. They’re smarter, better educated and superior to you and me, so you won’t find them at the local dive bar or out on dance floor at your typical night club…No, they live for those polaroid moments holding young brown children in disadvantaged, poverty stricken countries—so they can plaster it all over Instagram and FB and make you feel like you’re not contributing as much to society as they are. This is modern day liberal tourism gone wrong. The Ambassador—Tax payer funded travel to make inside deals that don’t benefit tax payers. Must have expensive suite, luxury accommodations, and reservations at the finest dining establishment in town. If the limo driver is late to the airport by more than 3 minutes he won’t get a tip. The Corporate Drone—My company pays for me to travel! The corporate drone pretends to love their job because the perks are just soooo great! Hey—I got to travel to Europe and Australia this quarter! Corporate drone will be spotted with a stack of receipt at the local coffee shop…Because they have to get that expense report in to their manager by 3pm eastern. Question: Why do shark tank companies always talk about how much sales they've had since being on the show and not how much profit?
Answer: That's a great question. The answer isn't clear but here's some ideas: 1. most of the companies are early stage ventures, so they probably don't have great scale, and therefore have low margins...they are on the show to improve just that. 2. they may be focused on growth and not optimizing for profit, so they focus on gross revenue. 3. the don't want to talk about profit, so they avoid the question, possibly because they have no profit. 4. contractual obligation—> they agree not to discuss profits before appearing on the show.

Question: How does the Gary Vaynerchuck content machine work?
Answer: It has nothing to do with tools or organization and everything to do with talent, work ethic, and talent. Did I mention talent? He also has a bit of an edge since he happens to run a digital agency with hundreds of employees but lets forget about that for moment. Gary is a walking talking content machine. People are curious about what he has to say because he has a magnetic energy, he knows what he’s talking about, and has a unique perspective that’s well outside of the feel good, woo woo, “find your passion” bullshit you hear from people building person brands. The number of posts per day, the number of people working on the project, the tools and back office shit–that’s a commodity. But the talent, know-how, and energy Gary brings (and **VALUE**) Gary brings to his audience is what counts.

Question: Did you ever board the wrong plane?
Answer: “FU*K!” the guy next to me yelled as he jumped out of his seat, bashing his head on the overhead storage. “I’m on the wrong f*cking plane!” …And then it occurred to me that no one checked my boarding pass and I’d been allowed to freely walk onto this aircraft without knowing if it was the correct flight. I scrambled to find my boarding pass hidden in the depths of my backpack. I was in the right seat. And I was sure I had been waiting at the correct gate. But the flight attendant just said “welcome to American Airlines flight (xyz) to Bogota, Colombia.” The guy next to me instantly freaked but I was more troubled by the collective look of disbelief on the faces around me. It turns out the flight attendant just made a mistake. We were going to Chicago, not Bogota. I think I would have preferred Bogota.
